review_text: Like the 12/02/24 review says, the prof doesn't really give us example problems of the material when we are first introduced to it. He also does sometimes skip steps in his lectures and makes some things sound obvious when they are not. The title of the class "Applied Harmonic Analysis: An Introduction to Signal Processing," can be somewhat misleading. The exams and lectures are mostly theoretical and the homework include some theory and some application (mainly in the form of MATLAB coding). I'll break down each of these 3 components: Lectures: Pretty theoretical especially towards the middle and end. Expect to know linear algebra pretty well (Math240 material, idt Math405/401 is necessary). Czaja is a good lecturer though in that his lectures are very structured and easy to follow. He posts his notes online and his notes are very detailed (almost too detailed, but like one reviewer said, he sometimes writes certain things are "easy to see" when they aren't). You should still go to class though because he does say things in lecture that aren't in the notes Exams: This is what most people have mixed feelings about. Like previous reviewers mention, if you can see the trick/gimmick on each question, the exams are easy, otherwise the exams can be tough. This, on top of the fact that the prof doesn't go over many examples/doesn't make practice exams, means the only "real" way to study for these exams is to try stuff out on your own and study the lecture notes rigorously. While there are some problems in the profs lecture notes that do help, some exam questions will catch you off guard and there's no real way to expect it. Averages on exams are in the 60-70% range. Homeworks: Mostly chill, some are theoretical but not egregious and others are just implementing stuff in MATLAB. Studying the homeworks can sometimes help for the exams too. Pretty sure most of the class did well on the homeworks Additional Info: His grading is so that your lowest 2 homeworks get dropped and lowest midterm (out of 3) gets dropped. For Fall 2024, he again implemented the policy where you can take the grade of all 3 midterms and the first 8 homeworks as your final grade, and not take the final. However, for Fall 2024 our third midterm was NOT take home (and was also the day we came back from Thanksgiving Break). TLDR: If you care about/enjoy the theoretical math that propels signal processing and data representation techniques, this class might be for you. If you don't mind spending time on your own investigating these theoretical aspects, this class is for you. Else, I can understand why some people are frustrated with the way this class is taught and you might be better off taking something less stressful.

I had a family emergency and Yoon granted me an extension and offered to help fix my code without even considering it for a second. You will excel if you build a relationship with Yoon, and I suggest starting early!! review_text: I may daresay Dr. Dachman-Soled might be one of the better, if not best, crypto professors, especially if you're interested in moving forward with cryptography in any aspect. Her expertise lies very solidly in the domain of the subject, and she emphasizes a lot of the theoretical games that any good cryptographer should be considering when creating a cryptographic algorithm, such as CPA or MacForge. The importance of this can't be understated; from a practical standpoint, it's true that cryptographic algorithms tend to stay pretty constant thanks to NIST standards and cryptographic libraries, but if you're interested in crypto research, these are ideas that are foundational to the subject that even published crypto papers get wrong. She's also one of the few crypto profs that goes over post-quantum crypto, which we're slowly (very, very, very slowly) migrating towards, meaning that if you're interested at all in the future of crypto algorithms, you should absolutely take 456 with her. I enjoyed the subject immensely. The B I got was mostly thanks to me skill-issuing the statistics (I hate statistics) which is a large part of the analysis done on cryptography, especially in regards to information theory. (I also hate linear algebra, which is what a lot of PQC is.) (I'm not very good at math.) That being said, the class is hard as all hell and I don't recommend it with her if you're looking for something easy. I also wish that she covered more of the applications of the crypto algorithms. It's a bit of a shame that we didn't even go over digital signatures even though they're one of the more common applications of asymmetric crypto. If there was a bit more emphasis on real-world cryptosystems, like multi-party computation systems, encrypted messaging channels, or even more discussion on PKI, that would easily elevate this class from a 4 to a 5. On a side note, loved the website. Lots of bells and whistles.

review_text: Prof. Carpuat seems like a very nice person, so I don’t want or intend to make personal criticisms or insults toward her — just share my experience with the class. First off, there is a lot of emphasis on memorization (even if she never directly admits it). It genuinely feels like the class is training us for a competitive memorization bee rather than machine learning. Instead of relying on memorization, there should be a broader and more diverse set of practice problems after each topic so students can actually understand and retain concepts through, you know, practicing. Students aren’t going to magically derive new ideas on the spot — especially not when the slides barely explain the material in the first place. If the foundational explanations are weak, you can’t expect students to perform theoretical acrobatics on an exam. The cheat sheet on exams isn’t really helpful either when you don’t know how to use it because the slides are bad. Am I supposed to analyze and figure out each slide on my own? Unfortunately, I can’t, because I have other classes and responsibilities (like job searching in this bad market). Also, the midterms are borderline impossible to finish on time; they feel like the SAT, except with fewer breaks and more panic. The point distribution is baffling: somehow a multiple-choice question can outweigh an open-ended one that requires actual reasoning. Grading is strictly “right/wrong,” and partial credit is treated like a rare mineral you have to mine via a regrade request on Gradescope. In regard to the TAs, they act as if they’re doing charity work by helping students or grading assignments. Guys, undergrads pay tuition. We don’t have funding or tuition remission like PhDs, so please take TA responsibilities seriously. The number of grading mistakes is honestly impressive in the worst way. And one TA is borderline dismissive toward students. Yes, we know you’re all busy revolutionizing research science with your “Einstein discoveries” and preparing your Silicon Valley IPOs, but TAing is still part of the job. Treating it like an unpaid internship doesn’t magically make it one. Her teaching style isn’t very effective. Every time she asks a question in class, it’s clear the majority of the room is lost. And while pre-class reading is important, the textbook she assigns does not clearly lay out the foundations of ML. She may think students are struggling because of the math, but that’s not actually the problem; the issue is the chaotic slides and unclear explanations. There’s an overwhelming amount of theory with very little practice to anchor any of it. Then there’s the SVM (or any other topic) situation. You’d expect a core ML topic to come with diverse practice problems. Instead, we get about 10 nearly identical questions across quizzes, problem sets, and practice exams. Same structure, same notation, same tiny subset of concepts. Meanwhile, the midterm features completely different SVM topics that only showed up in two or three theoretical slides. At this point, I genuinely can’t tell if this is intentional — like a way to force a “normal distribution” so fewer people do well — or just poor planning. The class is generally demotivating. You’d think that a course this central to AI would be taught with enthusiasm and would foster a real learning environment, but no. Instead, the class makes you feel like you’re not good enough because the focus is entirely on exams, not understanding. Why are there no projects? Because she’s convinced everyone will cheat using AI. Maybe instead of eliminating projects, design them so that AI isn’t enough to do the intellectual heavy lifting — just like in actual research, where a model spitting out code doesn’t magically produce hypotheses, perform data analysis, or make expert judgments. This class is just too much of emotional lifting, so I'm good with bare minimum of studying for the "right/wrong" final exam moving forward. I can't definitely go on with how disappointing this class has been but overall, the course doesn’t feel thoughtfully structured. It feels like something thrown together and held together with theory-heavy slides and a hope that students will just figure everything out on their own.

review_text: The instructor is terrible. In every single aspect of teaching, I would give her a 0/10. The study guide she made was 13 pages long, and she didn't finish it because it was "taking her too long". I'm not joking, she literally couldn't finish the study guide, which is just a list, a list, a fricking list of things we need to not just know, but master. review_text: First thing to note before anything else: this class is frustrating at times, and near the end will drag on. That being said, I enjoyed this math class and would recommend Jiwoong Jang as an instructor for the class. This class is in one of those huge Armory lecture halls and the seats fill quickly, so I recommend getting to class even just 5-10m early to reserve a good seat. Jang writes better than some math professors and his writing can be read from further back, but he mutters under his breath a lot when speaking and has an accent so you will want to be able to read the board well. Jang is also somewhat poor at answering questions, as he has a difficult time at explaining it in a different way than he wrote it. Negatives out of the way, this class is a pretty standard math class where you show up, take notes for an hour, study the material a few times a week, and take a quiz weekly. These quizzes are simple, short, and have their subject matter reviewed for 40 minutes before you take them in the discussion sessions. Jang is a very kind understanding guy, and he seems to genuinely care about the students in his class. Alongside this, he assigns multiple MATLAB projects throughout the semester that are extremely hand-holdy with generous deadlines and can be done without a sweat even with no prior coding knowledge. They serve only to boost your grade, help you somewhat understand the material more, and I heard from my friends in other sessions that Jang is the only one to do this type of assignment. My only recommendation is to get ready to study for the final, as that exam pulls no punches.

review_text: Spring of 2025 was the test run for Dr. Buchner's first semester doing in person microbiology exams, and I think this contributed to why the exams were like /that/. The second exam was prepared for us by some nice TAs. With the final, again, it was prepared for us by some nice TAs. I think the TAs did a lot of the heavy lifting. So, instead of using those classes to do a proper review, he just talked about the things he liked. I will admit I do find this stuff interesting, but I believe that being tested on it and wasting valuable class time on it is unfair. Unrelated to Dr Buchner: Lab definitely helped boost my grade. She was incredibly nice, and completely turned it around the second semester. I am not just saying that because it wasn't an easy A anymore. After talking with her, studying from past mistakes, taking notes and going beyond to understand content, and staying engaged in lectures—all things that should allow someone to do well in a course—it was still unreasonably difficult. Sana purposefully put questions that were of high difficulty, beyond what the course content really required (based on what other professors assessed who had been teaching for many more years). Her content was not aligned to any specific textbook, making it difficult to find additional practice problems that matched what she taught without lots of searching, as she provided no practice questions outside of the examples given in lecture. Also, during lecture, she'd spend a majority of the class talking about theory and derivations that we did not really need to know, while spending relatively little time on actually going over practice problems. Over an hour and 15 minutes, we could get through what another professor would've done in 20. She refused to curve, despite the averages being around 60% or lower (or around that, it's been a semester). Additionally, though she was nice during office hours sometimes, she was not a nice person. Her TAs, who were very helpful throughout the semester in discussions and supportive whenever we needed it, she accused of helping students cheat because they weren't collecting exams quickly enough in a 100+ person class where they needed to organize exams at the same time as receiving them. She promised extra credit to offset the poor performance in Exam 2, arguing that we should earn the extra points rather than be given a curve. She told us repeatedly that this would be applied to whichever assignment category this benefitted us the most, and if that were true, I would've earned an A. She ended up saying that was too complicated and just gave us a tiny amount of extra credit (the points we earned for extra credit were divided so that the grade increase wasn't too much) in an assignment category that affected our grades much less, relatively. I completely understand being annoyed at students taking advantage of your kindness in the first semester that you taught, but that is not a reason to be unfair to students the next semester. review_text: If you take this professor: - The MATLAB assignments are horrible. You are simply assigned problems and expected to figure them out yourself. Now, this wouldn't be too bad if the textbook were alright. But that isn't the case. In particular, the textbook you must use is so out of date that many of the features they teach you literally don't work in MATLAB anymore, and you're going to need to spend significant time searching the web and/or attending tutoring to get help on solving the problems. Make sure to start the MATLAB assignments early. On the bright side, based on grading statistics, almost everyone got a full score on all their MATLABS, so as long as you at least mostly solve all the problems, you should be fine. - There is no point attending his lectures, as he is the worst lecturer I have ever seen. He talks in a very soft, monotone voice, and rambles without an organized train of thought. It's hard to follow what he's saying, and many people (including me) got up and left in the middle of the first lecture. Your time is significantly better spent self-studying for this class. - Make sure to attend all discussions. The people who had Chirag as their TA seem to have raving reviews about him, but as someone who didn't have him as my TA, I can attest that the quality of discussions can vary wildly depending on who your TA is. On top of this, there usually isn't enough time to solve all discussion problems in the discussion section. For both these reasons, make sure to individually work through all discussion problem sets yourself. - Grillakis posts notes from David Levermore, but Levermore's notes are borderline unintelligible and unreadable, even if you are experienced in reading math-heavy papers. In my opinion, Levermore's ability to explain a topic, no matter how simple, is almost as bad as Grillakis's ability to lecture on a topic. Levermore's notes are good for one thing, and one thing only: they have a lot of practice problems, usually with decent explanations of the solutions. Many people will tell you that Justin Wyss-Gallifent's diffeq notes are very useful for self-studying. Aside from the occasional typo (and the rare provably untrue statement), this is true, but what they don't tell you is that HIS NOTES DO NOT COVER THE ENTIRE LAST 1/3 OF THE CURRICULUM. Neither do Grillakis's lecture slides, and, if I'm remembering correctly, neither do Levermore's notes (barring some exceptions, in particular Green's functions). This course provides you with (almost) no materials for all topics between the second midterm and the common final, and this nearly caused me a mental breakdown in the days leading up to the final. Which brings me to my most important point: - Get to know someone who has a different diffeq professor, and have them send you all of their resources and practice exams. If this isn't possible, at least go to the Guided Study Session for diffeq in the days leading up to the final and download all the materials they give you there. I personally learned the entire last 1/3 of the curriculum from a single practice exam with solutions that my friend (who had Francisco Arana Herrera) sent me, two days before the final. I had long been of the opinion that it doesn't matter what professor you take a class with, as you can always self-study your way to a good grade. Taking diffeq with Grillakis single-handedly convinced me otherwise. Although it is true that you can always self-study your way to a good grade, having a bad professor can add an unnecessary amount of stress, work, and overall mental burden, ESPECIALLY if you aren't even provided with the proper materials to study the topics yourself. But with that aside, if you work hard enough, it is indeed possible to succeed in this class. I personally got a full 100 on both midterms (for which the upper quartiles were 90 and 84 respectively), and I even ended up outscoring my friend on the final (albeit only because he made a careless mistake). But even with all the curves (all I know is my 96.7 became an A+) and relatively easy (depending on who you ask) midterms, if I could do it over again, I would without hesitation take a different professor, or even better yet, take diffeq from a community college.

I would recommend taking MATH 401 though to get more out of this course. If this is your first 400 level CS class (it was for me), it might be a little rough at the start but if this isn't then this course shouldn't be a problem. Also adding on to the point that understanding 100% of the math isn't crucial is that the midterm was fully conceptual, no code, no math. Another thing that he does well is he spends the first 10 minutes of every lecture reviewing the material from last class in a slightly different format with slightly different slides and this always helps everything click. Every now and then he'll do an even bigger review of the last couple classes or even from the start of the semester to show how everything ties together. review_text: For clarity, I'll quickly explain the class format. 5 assignments that are worth 40% of your grade with the lowest score being dropped, one midterm (that is awkwardly placed at about a third of the way through the semester) that is worth 20% of your grade, and a final that is "cumulative" and worth another 40%. There is also a hefty curve in the class which can be upwards of 6-7% some years -- typically depends on the difficulty of the exams that year. Regarding the assignments, they are pretty challenging. They often can take between 10-20 hours (especially dynamic programming one) and lots of work since each problem involves understanding all the underlying concepts, inventing/creating an algorithm, proving it works with some reasonable degree of certainty (instructors tend to be lenient about how "good" your proof is if you're right though), and proving it works in the runtime bound. Definitely start early, and definitely make frequent visits to office hours to bother the TA's and ask them to review through your work since ultimately they are the ones grading the assignments. Regarding the midterm, it was weirdly placed. The midterm was placed at the same time classes that typically have 2 midterms have their fist midterm (around end of first week beginning of second week of October). Otherwise, that midterm was relatively straightforward conent-wise -- those who didn't do well either couldn't brainstorm the gimmick to answer the question on the exam, or simply didn't review and study enough. The average on that exam was about a 68%. The final, in my opinion, was slightly harder. It covers a significantly higher breadth of topics than the midterm. In my opinion, the depth that each question goes into in the topic was a bit lower since most of the questions were very similar to questions on previous practices or other CMSC451 finals practices you could find online. The final on its own isn't that challenging, however, with much of the content being straightforward from the textbook. So long as you practice the standard questions, you really should be fine. The best part of Child's class is lectures. His lectures are just amazing. They are well put-together, easy to follow, and also have just enough "question the class to see what the class is thinking" but enough "let's guide through the class so we get some sh*t done". Laxman (the other well renowned and highly rated CMSC451 teacher who also taught Fall 2024) came and gave in a guest lecture, and I was absolutely surprised in the difference in quality between the lectures. Although Laxman's lecture wasn't "bad", it just really pointed out to me how much Child's lectures have an almost 3blue1brown feel because of how nice they flow. Some other misc things: he's pretty active on Piazza so that's really nice. Some of the TA's don't know a lot about these problems (and that follows because a lot of them naturally don't work in this field and might have other preoccupations), so they might also get stuck or not be able to help out on problems so try and exhaust all the TA's office hours and Child's office hours when stuck on homework. Child's expertise is in quantum algorithms so if you need anything with that or are interested, definitely feel free to talk to him about it. He tries to spend a lecture covering basic quantum algorithms at the end of the course but sometimes he doesn't have time to do that (like this semester), but regardless, you should look into it if interested. Overall, I had a lot of fun in this course and it's a definite recommend (even over other CMSC451 sections -- including Laxman's). While you might not necessarily get much practical implementation value out of the course, it's a lot of fun, and definitely molds your brain to become better and more versed in the world of reading and understanding algorithmic problems (which can be infinitely valuable when doing things like Leetcode or software interviews). If you have any math background or are interested in any algorithms stuff, definitely take the course!

review_text: Dave Mount is easily the best professor I’ve ever had. HOWEVER, Mount is an insanely generous grader, so even if you don’t see how to answer an algorithm question, he offers so much partial credit (more than I felt like I deserved) if you demonstrate even some knowledge of the base concepts. This class is really challenging and you will need to dedicate a lot of time to it, but I’ve learned so much and the help/resources Mount provides are more than enough to help you succeed.

review_text: Going into this class, I had heard a lot of positive reviews about Dr. Davis, and I also had a strong chemistry background (all As up to that point). First off, Dr. Davis is incredibly kind—honestly one of the nicest professors I’ve ever had. He explains concepts clearly, takes time during lecture to answer student questions, and you can tell he’s an expert in his field. That said, the class itself is somewhat disorganized. His notes aren’t great, and lectures can feel scattered. At times, he would lose his train of thought and jump to a new topic unexpectedly. On top of that, the class meets at 8 frickin AM, which made it so cheeks to attend, so I stopped going after the first couple of weeks. In terms of grading, your final grade is almost entirely based on exams, which is pretty standard for chemistry courses. The best part about Dr. Davis’s grading policy is that he allows you to drop one exam—including the final. The exams themselves are fair, and if you understand the material and complete the practice exams, you should be in good shape. The first midterm is very easy, and you should absolutely take advantage of it to buffer your grade. The only reason I earned an A in this class was because I did extremely well on the first exam. The second exam was by far the hardest for me, mainly because I wasn’t prepared for the jump in difficulty. Each exam gets progressively harder, so you definitely need to increase your studying as the semester goes on. The second exam ended up being my dropped exam. The third exam and the final were similar in difficulty, and I scored in the top 25% of my class. Dr. Davis also offers bonus points for completing practice exams—nine points total, with three points per midterm. I initially thought I would receive an A− since I narrowly missed the 90% cutoff, but Dr. Davis adjusted the grading cutoffs after the final, which ultimately earned me an A. For studying, I started about three days before each exam. I made a review packet based on his in-class notes (which was often my first real exposure to the material since I wasn’t attending lecture), made sure I fully understood the concepts, memorized key information, and completed two to three practice exams. If I could do it again, I would definitely make time to complete more of the practice exams to feel more confident going into the tests.
